# A DECLARATION OF THE INDEPENDENCE OF CYBERSPACE

*The founding document of a movement, kept whole and unaltered, with the
room's reading set after it rather than over it. It is held for what it
reached for and for the two things it got wrong: the fortification faced the
wrong way, and the world it declared did not stay separate. Both errors are
more useful now than the parts that were right.*

## THE TEXT, AS PUBLISHED

*A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace*, by John Perry Barlow.
Davos, 8 February 1996. Reproduced in full and unedited, under the Creative
Commons Attribution licence carried by the Electronic Frontier Foundation's
canonical copy.

Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel, I come from Cyberspace, the new home of Mind. On behalf of the future, I ask you of the past to leave us alone. You are not welcome among us. You have no sovereignty where we gather.

We have no elected government, nor are we likely to have one, so I address you with no greater authority than that with which liberty itself always speaks. I declare the global social space we are building to be naturally independent of the tyrannies you seek to impose on us. You have no moral right to rule us nor do you possess any methods of enforcement we have true reason to fear.

Governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. You have neither solicited nor received ours. We did not invite you. You do not know us, nor do you know our world. Cyberspace does not lie within your borders. Do not think that you can build it, as though it were a public construction project. You cannot. It is an act of nature and it grows itself through our collective actions.

You have not engaged in our great and gathering conversation, nor did you create the wealth of our marketplaces. You do not know our culture, our ethics, or the unwritten codes that already provide our society more order than could be obtained by any of your impositions.

You claim there are problems among us that you need to solve. You use this claim as an excuse to invade our precincts. Many of these problems don’t exist. Where there are real conflicts, where there are wrongs, we will identify them and address them by our means. We are forming our own Social Contract. This governance will arise according to the conditions of our world, not yours. Our world is different.

Cyberspace consists of transactions, relationships, and thought itself, arrayed like a standing wave in the web of our communications. Ours is a world that is both everywhere and nowhere, but it is not where bodies live.

We are creating a world that all may enter without privilege or prejudice accorded by race, economic power, military force, or station of birth.

We are creating a world where anyone, anywhere may express his or her beliefs, no matter how singular, without fear of being coerced into silence or conformity.

Your legal concepts of property, expression, identity, movement, and context do not apply to us. They are all based on matter, and there is no matter here.

Our identities have no bodies, so, unlike you, we cannot obtain order by physical coercion. We believe that from ethics, enlightened self-interest, and the commonweal, our governance will emerge. Our identities may be distributed across many of your jurisdictions. The only law that all our constituent cultures would generally recognize is the Golden Rule. We hope we will be able to build our particular solutions on that basis. But we cannot accept the solutions you are attempting to impose.

In the United States, you have today created a law, the Telecommunications Reform Act, which repudiates your own Constitution and insults the dreams of Jefferson, Washington, Mill, Madison, DeToqueville, and Brandeis. These dreams must now be born anew in us.

You are terrified of your own children, since they are natives in a world where you will always be immigrants. Because you fear them, you entrust your bureaucracies with the parental responsibilities you are too cowardly to confront yourselves. In our world, all the sentiments and expressions of humanity, from the debasing to the angelic, are parts of a seamless whole, the global conversation of bits. We cannot separate the air that chokes from the air upon which wings beat.

In China, Germany, France, Russia, Singapore, Italy and the United States, you are trying to ward off the virus of liberty by erecting guard posts at the frontiers of Cyberspace. These may keep out the contagion for a small time, but they will not work in a world that will soon be blanketed in bit-bearing media.

Your increasingly obsolete information industries would perpetuate themselves by proposing laws, in America and elsewhere, that claim to own speech itself throughout the world. These laws would declare ideas to be another industrial product, no more noble than pig iron. In our world, whatever the human mind may create can be reproduced and distributed infinitely at no cost. The global conveyance of thought no longer requires your factories to accomplish.

These increasingly hostile and colonial measures place us in the same position as those previous lovers of freedom and self-determination who had to reject the authorities of distant, uninformed powers. We must declare our virtual selves immune to your sovereignty, even as we continue to consent to your rule over our bodies. We will spread ourselves across the Planet so that no one can arrest our thoughts.

We will create a civilization of the Mind in Cyberspace. May it be more humane and fair than the world your governments have made before.

Davos, Switzerland

February 8, 1996

## I · WHY IT IS KEPT

The room already holds a chart for this kind of object. Kelvin proposed that
atoms were knotted vortex rings; he was wrong; and the tables of knots drawn
up to catalogue those atoms outlived the theory and became the mathematics
this work is built on. The guess died, the geometry survived, and the
geometry was the truth the guess was reaching for. That chart stands as
[The Vortex Atom](#/vortex-atom), and the discipline it names governs this
one.

A declaration is not a theory and cannot be falsified the way a physics can.
But it can be read against what followed, and when it is, the same pattern
appears: a reach in the right direction, arriving at the wrong object, whose
wreckage is worth more than a cautious correctness would have been. It
circulated further than any argument about networks before or since, and it
was overtaken by events within a decade. The shape of that overtaking is the
reason it is kept whole here rather than excerpted.

## II · THE FORTIFICATION FACED THE WRONG WAY

The Declaration names one adversary, and that adversary is the state. Its
frame is the frame of its decade: government as the threat to liberty, the
market as the force that would route around it. The information industries
appear once, and they appear as obsolete.

The capture came from that quarter and not the other. It did not arrive as
censorship or as law. It arrived as free services, and it took more ground
in ten years than any legislature has taken since.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it explains nearly every
feature of the network that followed. If a service is free, someone else
pays, and whoever pays chooses. Advertising requires attention; attention
requires engagement; engagement requires prediction; prediction requires
data; data requires surveillance; and surveillance requires scale. The feed,
the notification, the endless scroll, the real-name policy, the closing of
every open interface: none of these were technical decisions. Each is a
funding model expressing itself through an architecture.

This is why openness alone has never once been sufficient. Electronic mail
was decentralised and one provider holds most of it. The web was open and a
single browser engine effectively sets its rules. Syndication was free,
open, and unowned, and it lost anyway. Free and easy has defeated open and
difficult every time it has been tried, because a service funded by
attention can always be more free and more easy than one paid for by the
people using it.

The line about infinite reproduction at no cost was correct, and it did not
save anything. Distribution stopped being the scarce good, and attention
became it, and the same argument that freed the copy delivered the reader.

## III · THE SEPARATION THAT COLLAPSED

The second error runs deeper than the first. The Declaration asserts a world
apart: everywhere and nowhere, not where bodies live, a place whose legal
concepts cannot apply because there is no matter in it.

That premise did not merely fail. It inverted. There is no cyberspace now.
There is one world, carried in a pocket, and the network is a layer through
which ordinary life is conducted: work, money, medicine, courtship,
grievance, and the organisation of actual streets. A boundary drawn around
the digital in 1996 encloses, in this decade, nothing at all. The virtual
self was never immune, because it was never separable.

A movement that inherits the Declaration inherits this correction with it.
The aim is not a second world to escape into. It is instruments that serve
the only world there is, and the measure of such an instrument runs opposite
to the measure the platforms use: a tool for gathering people succeeds when
they leave it for one another, and time spent inside it is a cost rather
than a yield. That inversion is unavailable to any service funded by
attention, which makes it the one advantage a small work holds permanently.

## IV · WHAT THE ERROR TEACHES

The instructive part is not that Barlow was wrong. It is that he was wrong
in a specific and structural way: he fortified against the adversary of the
preceding decade, and the next one came from an unwatched quarter.

Anyone writing in this register now is likely making an error of the same
class, and by construction it cannot be seen from inside. Naming an enemy
dates a document the moment the enemy changes, and the enemy changes.

The defence available is not better prophecy. It is to build so that the
properties hold whoever arrives. Work held locally, keys held by the person
they name, systems that run with the network unplugged, and instruments that
can be copied entire and carried away: none of these depend on knowing who
the captor will be. They hold against a government, a corporation, a model,
or something not yet imagined, because they do not describe an opponent at
all. They describe a floor.

That is the reach the Declaration was making, stated in a form that does not
expire. Sovereignty was the right instinct. It was simply never available by
declaration, and it was never going to be defended at a border. It is
available, if at all, as a property of construction.

## PROVENANCE

*Set down 25 July 2026 at the architect's word, as an addendum to a founding
text of the movement this work belongs to rather than as a chart of the
deck. The Declaration is reproduced above in full and without alteration,
including its own spellings, under the Creative Commons Attribution licence
carried by the Electronic Frontier Foundation's canonical copy; the author's
words are his, and the errors named are named against the record of what
followed rather than against his intent. Everything after the text is the
room's own reading: the two errors, the funding mechanism traced to its
root, and the correction stated. The Kelvin discipline governing the entry
belongs to [The Vortex Atom](#/vortex-atom), and the shelf-mate this chart
was written to stand beside is [The Pro-Human AI
Declaration](#/pro-human-ai-declaration). The deck enters nowhere. Nothing
here predicts, and nothing here prescribes.*
